query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (2–3 wt%) of copper to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will improve its mechanical integrity by promoting grain refinement and grain-boundary strengthening while preserving its large field-induced caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 in bulk form exhibits a large caloric response via field‐induced phase transformation but is prone to cracking and poor mechanical integrity.
generation.intervention: Introduce 2–3 wt% Cu into the alloy composition followed by a controlled heat treatment to enable Cu segregation to grain boundaries and formation of coherent or semi-coherent nano-precipitates.
generation.conditions: Tested under applied magnetic and pressure fields near the caloric transition temperature, with mechanical loading (compressive tests in the tens to hundreds MPa range) similar to the baseline conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale Cu-rich precipitates at grain boundaries and a refined microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The minor Cu addition is expected to segregate at the grain boundaries during controlled cooling/heat treatment, which refines the grain structure and creates ductile intergranular phases. This microstructural modification improves crack resistance and enhances compressive strength by distributing internal stresses more uniformly, while the low concentration and coherent nature of these precipitates preserve the underlying crystallographic phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cu-doped alloy should exhibit a compressive strength exceeding previous benchmarks (targeting >218 MPa) along with retention (or a negligible change) in the caloric response (e.g., similar isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) compared to the pristine alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows a high caloric effect but suffers from cracking and lower mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is intended to operate under similar applied-field and pressure-field conditions and temperature regimes as the original tests, with mechanical loads in the tens to hundreds MPa range. The heat treatment process must be optimized to encourage beneficial Cu segregation without forming unwanted detrimental phases.
generation.uncertainty: While microalloying with Cu has demonstrated improved mechanical properties in related systems, the precise balance between enhanced compressive strength and possible slight shifts in caloric response remains uncertain without detailed processing optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and a second set with a 2–3 wt% Cu addition. Process both sets under identical melting and heat-treatment conditions designed to promote Cu grain-boundary segregation. Conduct compressive strength tests, fracture toughness measurements, and caloric effect measurements (such as isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under identical applied-field and pressure-field conditions near the caloric transition temperature.
measurements: Fracture toughness or crack propagation behavior
Caloric performance metrics (isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength and/or if the caloric response is compromised beyond a negligible margin relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). From this juncture, it is argued that the most stable composition is within the CrMnFeCoNiCu system rather than the CrMnFe

In this work, we have shown that an HEA film can be synthesized from a single partially spark-plasma-sintered target. Such use of single target sputtering was beneficial for synthesizing nanocrystalline films with low grain sizes and superior mechanical properties. The addition of Cu to the RHEA film was shown to increase the hardness and nanopillar compressional strength. The CuMoTaWV RHEA film showed an average hardness and nanopillar compressive strength of 19 ± 2.3 and 10 ± 0.8 GPa, respectively, which are ∼20% higher than those of the reported RHEA films in the literature. The high hardness and compressional strength of the reported film were attributed to nanocrystalline grain size and grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation. The wear behavior and adhesion of the CuMoTaWV film on a steel substrate were improved by annealing at 300 °C, and it showed improved coefficient of friction and wear resistance at RT and 300 °C. The reported results suggest that RHEA films can be beneficial for wear and nanopillar applications.

frame.system: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy in its as‐produced bulk form exhibiting a large caloric response (via field‐induced phase transformation) but prone to cracking and poor mechanical integrity
frame.goal: Achieve a single-material system that possesses both robust mechanical (crack‐resistance/compressive strength) and high caloric performance under applied field and pressure conditions, while remaining rare‐earth free
frame.limitation: The alloy’s intrinsic poor integrity (tendency to crack) which currently requires composite‐based interventions that improve compressive strength or heat transport individually but do not simultaneously preserve the caloric response
root_cause_cues: desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: The solution must use a single intervention (not a dual-phase composite)
The modified material must remain rare-earth free
Debe not sacrifice the large caloric response while improving mechanical integrity
frame.regime: Operation under combined applied-field and pressure-field conditions, subject to temperature regimes where the caloric phase transformation occurs (likely near the transformation temperature) and under mechanical loading conditions similar to the compressive tests reported (in the range of tens to hundreds of MPa)
prior_attempts: Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites that enhanced compressive strength (152–218 MPa) but may compromise thermal conduction or other aspects
Low-melting In composites that increased thermal conductivity significantly (over eightfold) but provided lower compressive strength (48 MPa)
frame.hypothesis: A promising single intervention is to microalloy the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with a minor addition (e.g., 2–3 wt%) of a ductile, rare‐earth–free element such as copper. The Cu atoms are expected to segregate to grain boundaries during controlled cooling or subsequent heat treatment, refining the microstructure and promoting the in-situ formation of coherent/semicoherent nano-precipitates. These structural modifications can impede crack initiation and propagation while maintaining the lattice transformation responsible for the caloric response.
frame.mechanism: The Cu addition encourages grain refinement and forms ductile grain-boundary phases that enhance toughness. It also helps distribute stress more evenly across the microstructure, thus increasing the bulk compressive strength. Importantly, because the amount is kept low and it segregates finely at the boundaries, the caloric phase transformation (and thus the caloric performance) remains largely unaffected.

expected_outcomes.mechanical: An increase in compressive strength exceeding the previously measured benchmarks (targeting >218 MPa) by suppressing crack propagation and enhancing ductility
expected_outcomes.caloric: Retention (or slight improvement) of the caloric response (e.g., in terms of entropy change or temperature span) compared to the unsubstituted alloy

frame.boundary_conditions: The intervention is intended to function under the same applied magnetic/pressure fields, temperature near the caloric transition, and mechanical loading as the original tests. The heat treatment must be optimized so that Cu segregates effectively without forming deleterious secondary phases.
frame.supporting_evidence: Similar microalloying strategies in other alloy systems (e.g., steels and shape-memory alloys) have demonstrated that minor additions of ductile elements can effectively enhance mechanical integrity (grain boundary strengthening and crack arresting) without impairing functional properties. Reports of improved toughness and strength via nano-scale precipitate engineering in multifunctional alloys provide a conceptual precedent.
frame.decisive_controlled_experiment: Prepare two sets of samples: one set as the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 and the other with 2–3 wt% Cu addition. Process all samples under identical conditions including optimized heat treatments to promote Cu segregation. Under identical applied-field and pressure-field conditions, measure the compressive strength, fracture toughness, and caloric effect (e.g., isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) for both sets. A falsifying result would be if the Cu-doped samples show no significant improvement in mechanical integrity (or reduced strength below the baseline) or if the caloric response is compromised by more than a negligible margin.

decision.trend: Early work in high-entropy and multi‐principal element alloys initially focused on thermal treatments and microstructural tuning (e.g., manipulating recrystallization and nano‐precipitate formation in alloys like CoCrNi and its variants) to enhance mechanical properties. Subsequently, researchers turned to composite and interface engineering approaches (using ductile epoxies, low-melting metals, or added phases like TiC and graphene) to improve strength or toughness. However, these interventions typically improved one metric (either mechanical integrity or thermal/caloric properties) at the expense of another. Studies such as PMC10056590 further demonstrated that minor compositional modifications—in this case, adding copper—can lead to non‐equiatomic optimized HEA systems with enhanced strength while retaining key functional properties.
decision.unsolved: There remains no single-intervention strategy that simultaneously reinforces the alloy’s mechanical integrity (i.e., preventing crack propagation and achieving compressive strengths >218 MPa) without diminishing its large field-induced caloric response, all while avoiding rare-earth elements.
decision.lever: Introduce a minor (2–3 wt%) Cu addition with controlled heat treatment to promote grain-boundary segregation and the formation of coherent/semicoherent nano-precipitates
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of employing subtle compositional adjustments—shown effective in related HEA systems (as in PMC10056590)—to achieve microstructural refinement. By using a ductile, rare-earth–free element, the technique is designed to enhance toughness and crack resistance without interfering with the caloric phase transformation, ensuring that both mechanical and caloric functionalities are preserved under applied-field and pressure conditions.
